name: Film Grain
basis: why: the picture is made of silver crystals, grain strongest in mid tones; how: toe and shoulder, stock balance, mid-tone grain, halation

lumenary.blurb: Silver halide, up close: grain that is strongest in the mid-tones, a soft shoulder in the highlights, halation, dust and a scratch or two.

facts.bestOn: Portraits and street scenes with mid tones

why: Film makes its picture from tiny silver crystals, and where there are few of them, or where they are nearly all exposed, the picture is smooth. In the middle tones the clumps show most. So grain is not uniform noise: it is strongest in the mid tones, weaker in deep shadow and bright highlights, and it picks up a faint colour from the dyes. A film stock also has its own tone curve and colour balance.
how: Lift the darkest level to a toe value and hold the lightest below a shoulder value, with a gentle S in between.
Apply the colour balance of the chosen stock: black and white, a warm portrait film, vivid slide film or cool night film.
Make grain from soft blobs at the grain size plus a fine speckle, with strength following a parabola that peaks in the mid tones.
On colour stocks give each channel 60 percent shared grain and 40 percent its own.
Add halation, a red-orange fringe from highlights bouncing through the film base, then dust, scratches and faded blacks.
history: Photographic film coated with light sensitive silver halide crystals replaced glass plates at the end of the nineteenth century. Kodak Tri-X, introduced in 1954, became a favourite of photojournalists for its grain and speed, and later stocks such as Fuji Velvia in 1990 and Kodak Portra in the late 1990s gave particular looks to colour. Film grain is still added to digital footage to make it feel organic.
terms: The light sensitive crystals that form an image on traditional film.
A glow around bright highlights caused by light bouncing back through the film.
The curved ends of a tone curve, where shadows and highlights are gently compressed.
paragraphs: A film stock is a recipe of three things: a tone curve, a colour balance and a grain. The tone curve here lifts the darkest level to a toe value and holds the lightest below a shoulder value, with a gentle S in between made by mixing a straight line (55%) with a smoothstep (45%). Four stocks are modelled: a black-and-white 400, a portrait colour film that is a little desaturated and warm, a vivid slide film, and a cool, grainy night film. The faded blacks slider then lifts everything toward grey by up to 12%, the milky shadows of an old print.

Grain is silver crystals clumped together, so it is not uniform noise. Its strength follows the parabola 0.2 + 3.2 l (1 − l), strongest in the mid-tones and weaker in deep shadow and bright highlights, where the film is nearly empty or nearly saturated. It is made of soft blobs (smooth noise at the grain size) plus a fine speckle (white noise). On colour stocks each channel receives 60% of a shared grain and 40% of its own, so the grain is faintly coloured. Halation is the red-orange fringe made when bright light bounces back through the film base: the picture is shrunk to one eighth, its highlights are kept and tinted, and the result is blown up and screened back. Dust, hairs and long scratches are drawn at random on top.

equations.note: t₀ is the stock’s toe and t₁ its shoulder.
Grain: ν smooth noise at grain size, r white noise, A = 0.27 × the amount slider × the stock’s grain factor.
Halation: the highlights of the one-eighth-scale picture, tinted red-orange (grey for black and white film).

presets.text: Black and white film with coarse grain looks like 1960s reportage.
Portra with light grain is warm and gentle.
Strong halation gives a glowing, dreamy red fringe.
